They find this downside-jump fear moves on its own, is not captured by the VIX level, and helps predict future equity returns, so it can flag nervous periods that a calm volatility reading misses. Puzzlingly, the premium falls or stays flat when risk rises, and a falling premium warns of higher risk ahead: a one-standard-deviation drop predicted about 3 points more S&P 500 realized volatility. Shorting VIX futures only while the premium was positive raised the Sharpe ratio from 0.57 (always short) to 0.87.

The effect lasted up to six months and fits the idea that informed traders act in options first. In the other direction, stocks that had risen tended to see their option implied volatility climb the next month even as realized volatility fell.

title: Derivatives and Market (Il)liquidity
learned: Huang, Yueshen and Zhang (JFQA 2023) build a theory model of how options and other non-linear derivatives change liquidity in the underlying stock or index. Informed investors who expect calm markets sell derivatives, and when buyers and sellers delta-hedge, the hedging trades dilute informed trading, so each trade moves the price less (liquidity looks better). Whether prices bounce back after moves depends on the derivatives' gamma, and the model warns that usual illiquidity measures may not line up with the liquidity risk premium once derivatives trade. It is pure theory with no numbers, and only the abstract was available.

title: Volatility Parametrizations with Random Coefficients: Analytic Flexibility for Implied Volatility Surfaces
learned: Standard curve formulas used to describe the implied-volatility smile (SABR, SVI) often cannot match very short-dated options, so the authors let one formula parameter be random, which turns the smile into a blend of two curves while staying arbitrage-free and fast to compute. On SPX options on 31 July 2024, the fitting error for the August 2024 expiry fell from 4.8e-4 (regular SABR) to 1.2e-5 (randomized SABR), and the needed randomness shrank as expiry got longer. A variant that randomizes the spot price fits the W-shaped smiles seen in near-expiry AMZN options on an earnings day (April 2018), when the market prices two possible outcomes.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Risks and Hedges of Providing Liquidity in Complex Securities: The Impact of Insider Trading on Options Market Makers
learned: This 2009 law-journal article by Stanislav Dolgopolov argues that options market makers lose more from insider trading than stock market makers, because they must quote both sides, carry leveraged non-linear positions and hedge their greeks (delta, gamma, vega), so a trader with secret news can pick them off before a big price jump. It reviews US court cases on whether options traders can claim damages and sketches how such losses could be calculated. It is a legal analysis with no market data or numbers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Local Estimation for Option Pricing: Improving Forecasts with Market State Information
learned: Federal Reserve researchers keep standard option-pricing models (Heston-Nandi GARCH and Heston stochastic volatility) but fit them giving more weight to past days that look like today, measured by VIX, recent realized volatility or simply how recent the day is. On S&P 500 options (14-183 days to expiry, 2011-2023, tested out of sample 2015-2023), this beat the usual equal-weight fit: for the GARCH model the VIX-weighted fit had the lowest implied-volatility forecast error with a Diebold-Mariano t-stat of -5.85 against the benchmark. Gains were largest in calm periods like 2017 and small after 2019 or in high-volatility stretches.

title: Profitability of selected 0DTE index options strategies
learned: This study back-tested two versions of a same-day (0DTE) Iron Condor on SPX options, using one-minute index and option prices over 12 months, and reports that both versions were profitable. The authors link this to 0DTE implied volatility being priced higher than the volatility that actually followed, so option sellers collected a premium. Only the abstract was available, so the size of the profits, costs and drawdowns is not known.
verdict: PROMISING (stress test: survived) : power 'inside_day' (base 11%): lowest-fifth days 2% vs highest-fifth 19%, Brier skill +3.4%, better than the base rate in 8/9 unseen years

title: Inferring Latent Market Forces: Evaluating LLM Detection of Gamma Exposure Patterns via Obfuscation Testing
learned: Regan and Xie fed an AI language model end-of-day SPY dealer-gamma numbers for 242 trading days of 2024, with dates and tickers hidden, and asked whether it saw dealer-hedging patterns; it flagged one 71.5% of the time (100% when given hints), and they say 91.2% of flags 'materialized'. But by their own concrete test (next-day move above 0.3% or intraday range above 1%) only 41.6% materialized, every single day in the sample was classed as negative gamma, and gamma only weakly predicted volatility two days later (p=0.042 at lag 2, not significant at lags 1, 3, 4, 5). Net profit after costs faded from +16 bps in Q1 to 0 by Q4.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.1%), better in 2/9 unseen years

title: Ultra-short-term volatility surfaces
learned: Options expiring within a week now make up about 70% of SPX option volume (2023), and their at-the-money implied volatility jumps around from one expiry to the next instead of forming a smooth curve, which classic pricing models cannot fit. Bandi, Fusari, Gazzani and Renò propose Edgeworth++, a jump model with flexible volatility plus a per-expiry shift, that prices all six shortest SPX expiries together quickly in closed form. On 247 trading days (May 2022-May 2023, sampled at 10:30, FOMC days removed) its average error was about 1.0 volatility point, against 1.9 for a two-factor Heston-jump model and 2.8 for a rough-Heston model, with roughly 37-38% of its prices inside the bid-ask spread.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Short‐Selling Bans Around the World: Evidence from the 2007–09 Crisis
learned: Beber and Pagano study the short-selling bans that regulators around the world imposed in 2007-09, using the fact that bans started, ended and applied differently across countries and stocks. Banned stocks became much less liquid: in the U.S. their median bid-ask spread rose 243% versus 54% for exempt stocks, and a covered-short ban added roughly 1.6-2.0 percentage points to spreads against a 3.9% average, with the damage about three times larger for stocks without listed options. Bans also slowed price discovery, especially in falling markets, and did not hold prices up, except possibly for U.S. financial stocks. The repo text covers the liquidity results and the start of the price-discovery section.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Crashes, Volatility, and the Equity Premium: Lessons from S&P 500 Options
learned: Santa-Clara and Yan pull two risk measures out of S&P 500 option prices every day: smooth (diffusive) volatility and the expected rate of crashes (jump intensity). Turned into a required return, the premium investors demand for these forward-looking risks averages 70% more than the premium for volatility that actually happened, and this option-implied equity premium significantly predicts later stock market returns. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 1149 signal days, hit 58.5% (always-long 58.5%), strategy +6.3 bps/day vs +3.8 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +2.5 bps/day, t=1.61, positive in 8/9 years

title: Specification Analysis of Option Pricing Models Based on Time‐Changed Lévy Processes
learned: The authors (Huang and Wu) compare many option-pricing models for S&P 500 index options that are built by speeding up or slowing down a jump process's clock. The best fit needs frequent small jumps in returns and two separate sources of changing volatility, one tied to the jumps and one to the smooth part of price moves. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no fit statistics are given.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Model Specification and Risk Premia: Evidence from Futures Options
learned: Using S&P 500 futures option prices from 1987 to 2003, the authors find strong evidence that both prices and volatility itself can jump, not just drift smoothly. They also find that investors pay a sizeable, statistically significant premium for protection against those jumps, and say this jump premium is key to understanding why options (especially puts) earn the returns they do. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so the size of the premia is not given.
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 1084 signal days, hit 57.7% (always-long 57.7%), strategy +2.8 bps/day vs +3.6 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds -0.8 bps/day, t=-0.50, positive in 5/9 years

title: Real-Time Probabilistic Pricing of Short-Horizon on-Chain Range-Prediction Markets
learned: The paper designs a pricing engine (TESSERA) for crypto 'range-prediction' bets where a user wagers the price stays inside a band for a few seconds to minutes, quoting a payout about once per second from a live price feed. Its volatility estimate is a recency-weighted average with a shock mode, and its anti-exploit rules (re-price on acceptance, kill stale quotes) drive stale-quote leakage from 0.78% to zero in simulation. On simulated data it was well calibrated (0.88% error at a 4.67% house margin), but on real 1-second BTC/USD ticks it failed at first (26% error) until one volatility-floor setting was re-fitted (5.5%), and jumps remained its main weakness.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.1%), better in 4/9 unseen years

title: Differential Machine Learning for 0DTE Options with Stochastic Volatility and Jumps
learned: The author trains a neural network to price 0DTE options and their Greeks under a model with both changing volatility and sudden jumps (Bates), learning prices and Greeks together so that one fast evaluation gives price, delta and gamma. A three-stage training that separately supervises the jump part cut the jump-term error from about 0.093 to 0.014 while keeping price errors similar, and adding jump-sensitivity labels brought the estimated jump intensity much closer to the truth (0.569 vs a true 0.60, compared with 0.739 without them). Everything is on simulated data; the author says applying it to real market data is future work, and notes gamma near the money remains the hardest thing to get right for 0DTE.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: From Arbitrage Removal to Density Extraction: A Model-Free Framework for Short-Dated Options
learned: Very short-dated options (a few hours to a week to expiry) have tiny premiums and wide bid-ask spreads, so mid prices are unreliable and quotes can even seem to allow free-money (static arbitrage) trades. The authors first strip out quotes that would allow such arbitrage at the actual bid and ask prices (ARIES), then fit the smoothest, least-assuming price distribution that stays inside every bid-ask range (SEDEx). On a synthetic Heston test the recovered distribution matched the true one to within about 0.0001 in price, and they apply it to SPXW options from 2012-2023 (five-minute quotes, snapshot 15 minutes before the close) to build short-dated volatility smiles.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: The Earnings Call Risk and Confidence Analyzer (ERCA)
learned: The authors argue that retail traders buy short-dated options before company earnings calls and lose money when implied volatility collapses after the release, even when they guess the direction right (the 'volatility trap'). They build a complex system (social-media activity model, sentiment indicator, machine-learning forecasters, quarter-Kelly sizing with a 15% drawdown stop) and report on 500 S&P 500 earnings events (2020-2026) that their sentiment-divergence score correlates with the size of the earnings surprise (Spearman 0.48). Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Temporal Obfuscation Testing for LLM Structural Reasoning: From Single-Day Dealer Constraints to Persistent Market Regimes
learned: The paper is mainly about checking whether a large language model really reasons or just remembers: it strips dates and tickers from dealer gamma exposure (GEX) data and asks the model to spot hedging patterns from the numbers alone, over 2,221 evaluations from 2020-2025. It reports 91.2% predictive accuracy on single-day patterns, and that raw strike-level data beat pre-computed GEX numbers by 30.8 points (92.3% vs 61.5%). For multi-day regimes, detection rose from 3.7% in 2021 to 100% in 2024 alongside 0DTE growth and GEX size growing from $3.0B to $20.3B, while the related strategy's Sharpe fell from 1.8 to 0.1, which the author reads as a real structure that is no longer profitable. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Forecasting the worst: is implied volatility forward-looking enough?
learned: The authors backtest a simple 1-day Value-at-Risk (the loss size you expect to exceed only rarely) on the S&P 500 using different volatility inputs. VaR built from the 30-day VIX underestimated risk in turbulent periods: losses broke the limit too often and the overshoots were too large. Preliminary evidence suggests the newer VIX1D, priced from 0DTE/1-day options, does a better job than VIX and the time-series alternatives. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so exact breach counts are not available.
verdict: TRANSLATION FAILED - RuntimeError: free AI daily limit reached

title: The Death of Fundamental Analysis? How Option Market Makers Now Dictate Spot Equity Prices
learned: This is a second listing of the same Vishal Chopra working paper on Gamma Exposure (GEX), framed as 'market makers now dictate spot prices'. It argues that dealers' mechanical delta hedging anchors prices when they are long gamma and accelerates moves when they are short gamma, and it describes trader tools such as the 'gamma flip' level, call walls and put walls as support, resistance and speed-change zones. No sample, test or numbers are given in the description. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: NO EDGE: 418 days, hit 46.2% (always-long 58.6%), avg -4.3 bps/day, t=-0.50, positive in 4/9 years

title: Institutional Equity Derivatives & Market Microstructure: Analyzing the Mechanics of Option Gamma Exposure (GEX) and its Empirical Impact on Underlying Asset Volatility
learned: This working paper explains Gamma Exposure (GEX): adding up option gamma across the chain tells you roughly how many dollars of stock dealers must buy or sell for each 1% move. When dealers are net long gamma they sell rallies and buy dips, which damps volatility and can pin price near big strikes; when they are net short gamma (often after heavy put buying) they chase the move and can amplify crashes or squeezes. The abstract describes formulas and mechanisms but reports no tested data, sample or numbers. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.533% (-0.4%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: Does Options Open Interest Pin the Underlying? Five Tests on 2,294 Trading Days
learned: Using 1.6 million near-expiry SPY option records matched to one-minute E-mini S&P futures over 2,294 trading days (2016-2025), the author runs five tests and finds no sign that big open interest 'pins' the index to a strike at expiry, unlike studies of the pre-2009 market. The only significant result (p < 0.001) goes the other way: days with the highest at-the-money open interest had about 16% wider daily ranges than days with the lowest. The author reads this as a shift from pinning to gamma-driven amplification, possibly tied to the growth of weekly and 0DTE options. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: power 'trend_day' (base 37%): lowest-fifth days 36% vs highest-fifth 35%, Brier skill -0.3%, better than the base rate in 6/9 unseen years

title: Deep learning in the stock market—a systematic survey of practice, backtesting, and applications
learned: This survey reviews deep-learning research on stock markets, keeping only studies that actually backtest their models so a practitioner could judge real-world use. The qualifying work falls into seven areas, mostly trading strategy, price prediction and portfolio management, with few studies on market simulation, stock selection, hedging or risk management; returns and volatility are the metrics that matter most for judging these models. The authors find reproducibility has improved but explainability is still weak, and say longer-horizon prediction remains a big unsolved problem. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no counts or performance figures are given.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Asymmetric Dynamics in the Correlations of Global Equity and Bond Returns
learned: Cappiello, Engle and Sheppard modelled how volatility and correlations of national stock and government bond indexes change over time, using 15 years of weekly returns (790 weeks, January 1987 to February 2001) and an asymmetric correlation model. Stock indexes get more volatile after bad news than after good news of the same size, while bond volatility shows little such asymmetry; yet both stocks and bonds become more correlated with each other after joint bad news, with stocks reacting more strongly, so diversification shrinks exactly when markets fall. After the euro's launch in January 1999 correlations jumped (bond returns inside the euro area became nearly perfectly correlated) while volatility levels did not break. The repo text was glyph-encoded and was decoded for reading.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.541% (-1.9%), better in 3/9 unseen years

title: Does herding affect volatility? Implications for the Spanish stock market
learned: Blasco, Corredor and Ferreruela measured herding (traders piling into the same side at the same time) in intraday Spanish stock trades, using the Patterson-Sharma herding intensity measure. They found herding raises volatility in a straight-line way across historical, realized and implied volatility, though the size of the effect differs by measure, and herding variables helped forecast volatility. The repo's text file is only the repository landing page (essentially the abstract), so no effect sizes are available.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Dilemma not Trilemma: The Global Financial Cycle and Monetary Policy Independence
learned: Rey shows there is one global financial cycle: capital flows, credit growth, bank leverage and risky asset prices around the world rise and fall together, and the cycle moves opposite to the VIX (low VIX = money pours in, high VIX = flows collapse). A single global factor explains about 25% of the variation in returns across 858 risky assets worldwide, and in her quarterly VAR a cut in the Fed funds rate is followed by a lower VIX after about 5 quarters and more credit flows after about 12 quarters; other studies she cites find Fed rate shocks explain roughly 20-30% of VIX variation at horizons beyond 7-10 quarters. Her policy conclusion is that with free capital flows, countries lose monetary independence even with floating exchange rates unless they manage capital flows or use macroprudential limits on leverage.
verdict: NO EDGE: 1215 signal days, hit 56.9% (always-long 56.9%), strategy +4.3 bps/day vs +4.1 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +0.2 bps/day, t=0.13, positive in 5/9 years [re-tested 19 Oct with drift-corrected test]

title: Central Bank Participation in Currency Options Markets
learned: The paper asks whether a central bank can calm an exchange rate by trading currency options instead of buying and selling the currency itself. Its key point is that if the central bank sells options, market makers end up long those options and their delta-hedging pushes against price moves (they sell rallies and buy dips), which dampens volatility; selling a strangle can also make a target zone more credible and may cost less than spot intervention, but it exposes the bank to unlimited losses. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no cost or volatility figures are given.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.534% (-0.5%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: The lead–lag relation between VIX futures and SPX futures
learned: The authors studied how VIX futures and S&P 500 futures move against each other minute by minute. When markets are calm the two are only loosely connected, but when volatility is high they move strongly in opposite directions and VIX futures tend to move first, with S&P futures following. The lead is so short that, after transaction costs, it could not be turned into a profitable strategy; whichever market is relatively more liquid tends to lead, and market-maker hedging also shapes the relation. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no correlation or lag figures are given.
verdict: NO EDGE: 1041 days, hit 48.4% (always-long 55.1%), avg -8.3 bps/day, t=-1.51, positive in 2/9 years

title: Price Formation and Liquidity in the U.S. Treasury Market: The Response to Public Information
learned: Fleming and Remolona studied how US Treasury prices, volume and bid-ask spreads react to major macro announcements. In a brief first stage the price jumps almost instantly while trading volume actually drops and spreads widen sharply, showing prices can reprice to news without much trading. In a longer second stage volume surges, volatility stays elevated and spreads remain somewhat wide as traders reconcile their different readings of the news. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no timing or size figures are given.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.531% (-0.0%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: An Empirical Investigation of Continuous‐Time Equity Return Models
learned: Andersen, Benzoni and Lund fitted continuous-time models to daily equity-index returns and found that a realistic model needs both stochastic (changing) volatility and sudden jumps, with jump frequency that can vary over time. Volatility shocks are strongly negatively tied to returns, so falling markets come with rising volatility (the leverage effect). These same features line up with what index option prices show, such as steep put skew, meaning the options market prices them. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no parameter values are given.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.2%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: By Force of Habit: A Consumption-Based Explanation of Aggregate Stock Market Behavior
learned: Campbell and Cochrane build a model in which people judge their well-being against a slowly moving 'habit' level of consumption, so they become much more risk-averse in bad times when consumption falls close to that habit. This single feature explains why stock prices rise in booms and fall in busts, why high prices predict low returns over long horizons, and why stock market volatility is higher in downturns, and the model tracks much of the history of US stock prices using only consumption data. The repo's text file is unreadable scanned OCR, so this summary is from the abstract only.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.530% (+0.2%), better in 3/9 unseen years

title: Betting against beta
learned: Frazzini and Pedersen argue that many investors cannot borrow, so they buy high-beta (extra-jumpy) assets to get more market exposure, which bids those assets up and leaves them with lower risk-adjusted returns. A 'betting against beta' portfolio, long leveraged low-beta assets and short high-beta assets, earned significant positive risk-adjusted returns in US stocks, 20 international stock markets, Treasuries, corporate bonds and futures. It does badly when funding conditions tighten, and tighter funding pushes betas toward one. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no return figures are given.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Carry Trades and Currency Crashes
learned: Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen show that the currency carry trade (borrow in low-rate currencies like the yen, invest in high-rate ones like the Australian dollar) earns small steady gains but carries crash risk: its returns are negatively skewed, and across currencies the link between interest-rate gap and skewness is very tight (R-squared of 81%). The crashes come from sudden unwinds when risk appetite and funding liquidity dry up, for example in weeks when the VIX or the TED spread rises. After carry losses, speculators hold smaller positions and pay more for crash insurance (risk reversals), and future crash risk actually falls. Read from the repo's full text.
verdict: NO EDGE: 211 days, hit 51.2% (always-long 51.2%), avg -15.8 bps/day, t=-0.98, positive in 4/9 years

title: Safe Haven Currencies
learned: Ranaldo and Söderlind used high-frequency exchange-rate data from 1993 to 2008 and a factor model linking currencies to stocks, bonds, volatility and liquidity. They find that the Swiss franc and Japanese yen strengthen against the US dollar when US stocks fall, US bond prices rise and FX volatility increases. This safe-haven behaviour shows up from a few hours to several days, grows non-linearly with volatility and in crises, and was especially strong for the yen in 2008. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Intraday Price Formation in U.S. Equity Index Markets
learned: Hasbrouck studied where prices are actually discovered among the instruments that track U.S. stock indexes: floor-traded futures, E-mini futures, ETFs and sector ETFs. For both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100, most price discovery happens in the E-mini futures, meaning futures tend to move first and ETFs like QQQ follow. For the S&P 400 MidCap it is shared between the regular futures and the ETF, and SPY leads the sector ETFs far more than they lead it. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no numeric shares are given.
verdict: TRANSLATION FAILED - formula gives too little usable data

title: The Flash Crash: High‐Frequency Trading in an Electronic Market
learned: Kirilenko, Kyle, Samadi and Tuzun used audit-trail, trade-by-trade data from the E-mini S&P 500 futures on May 6, 2010 (the Flash Crash) and the three days before. During the crash a large automated sell program was executed very quickly, and the most active non-designated intermediaries, classified as high-frequency traders, did not change their trading pattern as prices fell: they neither stepped in to absorb the selling nor clearly pulled away. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no further numbers are available.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Momentum crashes
learned: Daniel and Moskowitz show that momentum strategies (buy recent winners, short recent losers) usually pay well but occasionally suffer long, painful losing streaks called momentum crashes. These crashes are partly predictable: they happen in panic states, after the market has fallen and when volatility is high, and they coincide with sharp market rebounds that lift the beaten-down losers. A dynamic version that scales momentum down when its forecast mean is low and its variance high roughly doubled the alpha and Sharpe ratio of plain momentum. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 1805 signal days, hit 54.7% (always-long 57.2%), strategy +5.2 bps/day vs +4.2 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +1.0 bps/day, t=0.44, positive in 7/10 years

title: Does Net Buying Pressure Affect the Shape of Implied Volatility Functions?
learned: Bollen and Whaley show that implied volatility moves with public order flow: when more customers buy options than sell them, implied vol rises, so the shape of the volatility smile is partly driven by demand, not only by expected risk. For S&P 500 index options the biggest driver is buying pressure in index puts, while for single-stock options it is call demand. Delta-neutral option-writing strategies earned abnormal returns roughly matching how far implied vol sat above realized vol. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no specific numbers are available.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.2%), better in 4/9 unseen years

title: Can Large Language Models Beat Wall Street? Unveiling the Potential of AI in Stock Selection
learned: MarketSenseAI uses GPT-4 to read news, fundamentals, price trends and macro data and issue buy/hold/sell calls on S&P 100 stocks with written explanations. Over a 15-month test it reported excess returns of 10% to 30% and a cumulative return of up to 72%, with risk similar to the market. The test is short and covers a single period, and the paper is by the framework's own developers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Risk Everywhere: Modeling and Managing Volatility
learned: Using high-frequency data on more than 50 commodities, currencies, equity indices and bonds over 20+ years, the authors (Bollerslev, Hood, Huss and Pedersen) find that realized volatility behaves in very similar ways across markets. Fitting realized-volatility models jointly across many assets (panel estimation) gave better out-of-sample risk forecasts than fitting each asset alone, with significant economic gains in a utility-based test that also accounts for trading costs. The abstract gives no specific error numbers.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.533% (-0.3%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: Book-to-Market, Mispricing, and the Cross Section of Corporate Bond Returns
learned: Corporate bonds whose book value is high relative to their market price tend to earn more later: senior bonds, even investment grade, in the top 20% by this ratio beat the bottom 20% by about 3-4% a year after controlling for yield, spread, rating, duration, liquidity and past returns. The edge fades when trading is delayed and appears even where risk differences are small, which the authors read as mispricing rather than compensation for risk.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Frictions as a Constraint on Tax Planning
learned: This law-review article argues that narrow tax reforms aimed at specific tax-avoidance tricks work only when 'frictions' (fees, accounting or regulatory treatment, credit risk) make the workaround costly, and that sharp, all-or-nothing frictions deter end-runs best. It compares two US rules on derivatives, Section 1259 (constructive sales of appreciated stock) and Section 1260 (using derivatives to mimic hedge-fund ownership), which use almost the same wording yet drew different taxpayer responses because of differing frictions.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Finance-Informed Operator Learning for Option Pricing with Quantum-Compatible Realizations
learned: The authors train a neural network to price European options quickly under a local-volatility model by letting it learn only a correction on top of a Black-Scholes starting price, with a layer that keeps prices within no-arbitrage bounds. On test data from the same model family it cut overall relative pricing error by nearly ten times versus plain neural-network baselines, but on real index-option quotes it stayed accurate without retraining while still not beating the plain Black-Scholes formula on the same inputs. A 'quantum-compatible' version is also described, with no speed-up claimed.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Option Volume and Stock Prices: Evidence on Where Informed Traders Trade
learned: This classic paper (Easley, O'Hara and Srinivas) models informed traders choosing between the stock and its options, and shows when they prefer options, for example for the leverage. Testing with intraday option data, the authors find that option volume split into bullish ('positive', such as call buys and put sells) and bearish ('negative') trades carries information about where the stock price goes next. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning
learned: This well-known study (Gu, Kelly and Xiu) compares machine-learning methods for forecasting stock returns and finds that trees and neural networks beat standard regressions, in some cases doubling the performance of the best regression-based strategies. Their edge comes from capturing nonlinear interactions between predictors, and every method agreed that the strongest signals are variations on momentum, liquidity and volatility. The abstract gives no other specific figures.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.1%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: Cross‐Market Convergence Trading in Options Order Flow
learned: The authors separate options order flow driven by arbitrage-style 'convergence' trading (using matched calls and puts to build synthetic stock or futures positions when options are mispriced against the futures or spot market) from flow driven by traders with private information. This convergence flow grows as the options-futures mispricing widens and predicts returns in the related market in the opposite direction, unlike informed flow. Foreign investors mostly respond to options-versus-futures mispricing and domestic investors to options-versus-spot mispricing, and traders react more to spot underpricing than overpricing, consistent with limits on short selling.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: LiveOption: Evaluating LLM Agents in Structured Option Trading with Nonlinear Payoffs
learned: LiveOption is a test bed where six AI language-model agents traded options live in three tasks: hedging or covered-call overlays on stocks, earnings bets, and intraday 0DTE trading over 102 sessions. None beat simply holding the stock in the overlay task, every model had a negative median return on earnings bets, and in 0DTE each model lost on 62-76 of the 102 sessions with medians of -3.20% to -0.26% per session. The few positive 0DTE averages came from a handful of big winning days and turned negative once the real bid-ask half-spread was charged, mainly because agents kept paying time decay (theta) on bought options.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Empirical Performance of Alternative Option Pricing Models
learned: This classic study (Bakshi, Cao and Chen) builds an option model where volatility, interest rates and sudden jumps can all vary, and tests simpler versions against it on S&P 500 options. Adding changing volatility and jumps matters most for pricing options accurately and for making the implied numbers line up with actual market behavior. For hedging, though, a model with changing volatility alone worked best; the abstract gives no specific error numbers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Harvesting the Volatility Risk Premium: A Learning-to-Rank Approach
learned: The author uses a machine-learning ranker each morning at 10:00 ET to choose which of eight same-day (0DTE) SPX short puts to sell, from 5-delta to 45-delta, or to skip the day, with position size scaled up when 0DTE implied volatility is rich versus recent realized volatility. After margin, fees and bid-to-mid fills, the 2025 hold-out year showed Sharpe ratios of 4.31-5.76 and a -2.28% max drawdown, versus 1.90-3.11 in the 2021-2024 walk-forward, and returns rose with realized volatility. Most of the edge came from choosing the strike and when to skip; the extra risk controls added only 0.54 Sharpe, and the hold-out is a single year.
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 1145 signal days, hit 58.5% (always-long 58.5%), strategy +7.0 bps/day vs +3.8 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +3.2 bps/day, t=2.09, positive in 7/9 years

title: The Synergistic Impact of AI-Driven Strategies on Retail Options Trading within the European Derivatives Market: A Comparative Analysis of Liquidity and Market Efficiency
learned: This descriptive study compares US and European index options and argues that AI trading tools work better where markets are deeper: SPX trades about 1.2 million contracts a day versus about 300,000 for Euro Stoxx 50, with spreads of roughly 0.25% versus 0.40%. It cites options volume rising 18% in the US versus 9% in Europe after CPI releases and claims AI reduces retail behavioral biases, but this rests largely on industry reports rather than a tested model.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: A bid–ask constrained calibration framework for 0DTE SPX option pricing rough versus jump–diffusion volatility models
learned: The authors fit four 'rough volatility' models and one simpler jump model to intraday SPX same-day (0DTE) volatility smiles over five days, counting a fit as good only if model prices land inside the bid-ask spread. One rough model (QRH+) fit best on days with a sharply curved downside smile, but the simpler jump-diffusion model matched or beat every rough model on the other days and on average. The takeaway is that fancy rough-volatility models are not required to price 0DTE options well.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Where Does the Hedging Error Go? A Greek-by-Greek Decomposition for At-the-Money 0DTE Options under Heston
learned: The authors split the hedging error of at-the-money same-day (0DTE) options into seven Greek pieces across 1,015 SPY sessions and find gamma explains about 66% of the error's variance and vega about 38%; a delta-hedged position lost 2.41 basis points per session on average (t = -8.87). Most of the error cannot be hedged away by trading faster: about 86% of SPY's one-minute error (85% for SPX) is a fixed floor, and hedging every 10 seconds on tick data still leaves 93-98% of it. QQQ and NDX showed the same ranking, with gamma the biggest source.
verdict: DOESN'T FIT MY DATA - needs intraday option and stock prices, as well as dealer gamma positions, which are not available in the provided data

title: A New Star Is Born: Does the VIX1D Render Common Volatility Forecasting Models for the US Equity Market Obsolete?
learned: VIX1D is Cboe's index of how much the S&P 500 is expected to move over just the next day, built from the shortest-dated (largely 0DTE) options. The authors find it usually sits below the 30-day VIX but jumps around more, drifts upward during the trading day, and on average overstates the next day's actual move because it contains a risk premium. After a simple adjustment for that premium, VIX1D alone forecast next-day S&P volatility more accurately than the standard HAR forecasting models (the abstract gives no exact error figures).
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 1257 sell-vol + 838 buy-vol trades on real QQQ option prices, avg -8.0 bp of QQQ per trade (placebo avg -4.9, p=0.917), halves -8.7/-7.2, win 47%, worst -973 bp, positive in 1/9 years, sell trades return -3.9% of max risk; 36% of its sell days are high-gamma days (the known edge)

title: Revisiting local expansions for zero days-to-expiry option pricing
learned: Same-day-expiry (0DTE) options are hard to price because over a few hours prices move in jumps and lopsided ways that the normal bell-curve model misses. The authors price them with a fast 'local expansion' formula that adds corrections for skew and fat tails, and find that letting jumps follow a fat-tailed (tempered stable) shape prices SPX 0DTE options clearly better than assuming bell-shaped jumps; the method also held up on DAX and Euro Stoxx 50 0DTE options. The abstract gives no specific error numbers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Retail Trading in Options and the Rise of the Big Three Wholesalers
learned: Retail trading in US options has surged and now exceeds 60% of total market volume, helped by payment for order flow, and nearly 90% of that payment comes from three wholesalers. Using new trade flags to isolate wholesaler-executed trades, the authors build a measure of retail options activity that drops during brokerage outages. Retail traders favor cheap weekly options with an average bid-ask spread of 12.6%, and they lose money on average.
verdict: DOESN'T FIT MY DATA - needs intraday options trade data with wholesaler flags

title: Illiquidity Premia in the Equity Options Market
learned: This peer-reviewed paper (Review of Financial Studies, 2017) studies whether less liquid equity options earn different returns than liquid ones. The queue held no real abstract and the full text could not be opened (the site blocks automated reading), so no results or numbers could be checked in this session. Nothing more is claimed here.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: An Empirical Analysis of Stock and Bond Market Liquidity
learned: Modelling bid-ask spreads, depth, returns, volatility and order flow in stocks and Treasuries together, the authors find that liquidity and volatility shocks in the two markets are significantly correlated, so common forces drive both. Volatility shocks help predict later changes in liquidity, and in crises monetary easing goes with better liquidity. Money flowing into government bond funds forecasts bond market liquidity. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Option Return Predictability
learned: For single-stock options, the return to writing delta-hedged calls can be predicted from company traits: it is lower for high-priced, more profitable firms and higher for firms with lots of cash, volatile cash flows, new share issuance, distress risk and analysts who disagree. Long-short option portfolios built this way had annual Sharpe ratios above two and stayed profitable after trading costs. Two option-specific factors explain the profits; ordinary stock risk factors do not.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: The Determinants of Stock and Bond Return Comovements
learned: Using a model that ties stock-bond co-movement to interest rates, inflation, growth, cash flows, risk aversion, uncertainty and liquidity, the authors find that macro fundamentals explain little of how stocks and bonds move together; liquidity measures matter more. Macro factors help explain bond volatility, while the variance premium is key for explaining stock volatility. The model mostly fails to fit the stock-bond covariance itself. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Time Series Momentum
learned: Across 58 liquid futures (equity indexes, currencies, commodities, bonds), an asset's own past 1-12 month return predicts its next month: winners keep rising and losers keep falling, with some reversal over longer horizons. A diversified portfolio of these trend trades earned strong returns with little exposure to normal risk factors and did best in extreme markets. Speculators profit from it at the expense of hedgers.
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 2227 signal days, hit 56.4% (always-long 56.5%), strategy +3.4 bps/day vs +5.4 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds -2.0 bps/day, t=-0.74, positive in 4/10 years

title: Risk Premia in the Bitcoin Market
learned: Bitcoin is far more volatile than the S&P 500 and its options carry a larger variance risk premium (sellers of volatility are paid more). Most of the S&P 500's equity premium comes from mildly negative return days, while for Bitcoin those moderate down moves explain only about a third of its premium. Bitcoin's premia shift between two regimes: in calm markets investors pay more for variance and upside, and in volatile markets the premium is more balanced and smaller.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: High-Frequency Trading and Price Discovery
learned: High-frequency traders help prices find their correct level: their aggressive (liquidity-taking) orders trade in the direction of lasting price changes and against temporary mispricings, even on the most volatile days. Their passive quotes, on the other hand, tend to get picked off by better-informed traders. Their trading direction predicts price moves only over seconds and is tied to public news, market moves and order book imbalance.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Demand-Based Option Pricing
learned: Because dealers cannot hedge options perfectly, heavy end-user demand for an option pushes its price up, by an amount tied to how much of its risk cannot be hedged away. Using data on actual dealer and end-user positions, the authors show end users are net long index options, especially out-of-the-money puts, which helps explain why index puts look expensive and why the volatility smirk exists. In short, skew is partly a price of demand, not only a forecast of crashes.
verdict: DOESN'T FIT MY DATA - needs intraday option order flow data to measure end-user net demand by strike

title: Informed Trading around Stock Split Announcements: Evidence from the Option Market
learned: Looking at option implied volatility around stock-split announcements, the authors find that option traders correctly expect a stock to get more volatile after it splits. There is only weak evidence that options traders anticipate the positive price drift splitting firms tend to show. The option measures help predict post-split volatility levels and changes, but not returns.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Machine Learning-Based Latency-Aware Smart Order Routing for U.S. Treasury Securities
learned: The authors built a machine-learning order router for US Treasuries that tries to account for quotes going stale while an order travels to a venue, and tested it on a simulated order book calibrated to FRED yield volatility. Although the classifier scored 80.1% accuracy, the router beat a simple best-price router on only 2.2% of test rounds and was actually slightly more expensive (6.561 vs 6.548 basis points, t = -3.86). The honest lesson: a high-accuracy model can still make worse decisions when it is confidently wrong on the cases that matter.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Volatility of Volatility and Leverage Effect from Options
learned: The paper builds model-free estimators of how much volatility itself moves around ('vol of vol') and of the leverage effect (prices falling as volatility rises), using high-frequency prices of short-dated options. It extracts spot volatility from the options and corrects for the noise in option quotes. It is a statistics/methods paper: it shows how to measure these quantities precisely, not a trading result, and the abstract has no market numbers.
verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.534% (-0.5%), better in 3/9 unseen years

title: Decomposing the Theta Cliff: A SIMDEC Filtering of Asymptotic Time-Decay in Long-Call Options with a Real-Money Intraday Illustration
learned: This paper proposes scaling the normal Black-Scholes theta (time decay) by a factor that depends on the stock's sector and market regime, found with a sensitivity-analysis method called SIMDEC. Its main 'evidence' is three real-money long-call positions tracked through eleven intraday snapshots plus output from the author's own AI pipeline. There are no clear performance numbers, and the sample is far too small to show that the adjusted theta predicts anything.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Uncovering the asymmetric information content of high-frequency options
learned: The authors split the high-frequency moves of option prices into up-moves and down-moves (semivariances) and signed jumps, using SPY options and 15 single stocks. The downside moves of out-of-the-money calls and the upside moves of OTM puts help predict future volatility, the variance risk premium and next-month excess returns, beyond plain total option volatility. A volatility-timing strategy built on these measures gained up to 206 basis points a year out of sample for a risk-averse investor.
verdict: DOESN'T FIT MY DATA - The idea requires intraday OTM call and put option prices to compute realized semivariances, which are not available in the provided dataset (only end‑of‑day surface metrics are present).

title: Stock Market Uncertainty and the Stock-Bond Return Relation
learned: This older study links daily stock and Treasury bond moves to stock-market uncertainty, measured by index option implied volatility and unusually high trading volume. When implied volatility is high, stocks and bonds tend to move less together in the following period, and on days when implied volatility jumps, bonds tend to do well relative to stocks (a flight to safety). In plain terms: bonds diversify a stock portfolio best exactly when fear is high. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Deep hedging 0DTE options
learned: Using high-frequency SPX option data with real transaction costs, the authors train a reinforcement-learning agent to delta-hedge 0DTE options and find it beats standard Black-Scholes delta hedging at that horizon. The learned hedge kept working during the COVID-19 crash even though it was trained only on calm periods, and the paper also studies how it behaves around price jumps. The abstract gives no headline numbers for the size of the improvement.
verdict: DOESN'T FIT MY DATA - needs intraday option quotes and trades, as well as a reinforcement learning model implementation

title: One Premium in Four Disguises: Volatility Arbitrage, Implied Correlation and the (Apparent) Decay of the Dispersion Premium, 2006–2026
learned: Testing 2006-2026 data, this paper finds that four popular 'volatility arbitrage' trades (implied-vs-realized, VIX calendar, dispersion, skew-gated short vol) are really the same bet: each has a 0.71-0.95 daily correlation with simply shorting VIX futures, and none earns a significant extra return after correcting for testing many variants (best t-stat 2.16, failing a Holm test at p=0.09). The Cboe SKEW index was neither a source of return nor a reliable warning sign. The only add-on that held up out of sample was sizing short-vol positions in proportion to VIX (Sharpe 0.57 to 0.79), and even that is still just the plain variance premium.
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 258 signal days, hit 44.2% (always-long 55.8%), strategy -0.7 bps/day vs -0.9 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +0.2 bps/day, t=0.16, positive in 2/9 years

title: Arbitrage Scenario in India's Option Market - A mathematical modelling breakdown
learned: Using Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty minute and tick data from January 2025 to April 2026, this self-published paper argues that big institutional selling 'slams' on Wednesday/Thursday expiry afternoons set off retail stop-loss cascades, with a window of about 180-300 seconds between the slam and the peak of the cascade. It claims its 18-model 'Threshold Causal Calculus' suite was right 68.2% of the time during the March 2026 volatility spikes and cut slippage by 85.8% compared with moving-average crossovers. The claims are big, the method is vaguely described, and the comparison is only against a weak baseline.
verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Overcoming Execution Drag in Volatility Harvesting: Hysteresis and Partial PCA Orthogonalization
learned: A self-published (not peer-reviewed) Nifty50 study shows that a volatility-risk-premium strategy that looked good on paper (17.85% gross, Sharpe 1.84) turned into an 18.5% net loss once the cost of constantly re-hedging delta and slippage were counted. Only re-hedging less often (a 'deadband' that ignores small delta changes) and stripping out the index's main market factor brought it back to a claimed 11.44% net, Sharpe 2.03. The takeaway for a retail trader: hedging and trading costs can wipe out an options edge entirely, so trade less often and count costs first.
verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.1%), better in 5/9 unseen years
